Jest: the Test Runner

describe, it, and expect — the vocabulary of a test file, plus npm test wired up to run them.

Writing "run this code and check the result" by hand for every test would be its own chore — a test runner is a tool that finds test files, runs each one, and reports pass/fail for every check inside it. Laravel/PHP's equivalent is PHPUnit; this project uses Jest, the most common choice in the Node ecosystem.

A Jest test file groups checks using three functions — none of them need importing, Jest makes them globally available while tests run:

describe('a group of related tests', () => {
  it('describes one specific behaviour', () => {
    expect(1 + 1).toBe(2);
  });
});
  • describe names a group of related tests — usually one per function or module.
  • it (or its alias test) is one individual test — its string argument should read like a sentence describing the expected behaviour.
  • expect(actualValue).toBe(expectedValue) is an assertion: it passes silently if true, and fails the test (with a readable diff) if not. .toBe is one of many matchers — you'll meet a couple more shortly.

Back in Figure 1.1, package.json's "test" script was a placeholder. It now actually runs Jest:

"test": "node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/jest/bin/jest.js"

That --experimental-vm-modules flag is only needed because of a choice made back in Week 1's very first topic: this project uses ES modules ("type": "module"), and Jest's support for running ES modules directly (rather than the older CommonJS require) is still marked experimental in Node. Running npm test will print an ExperimentalWarning about it — that's expected noise, not a bug, and safe to ignore.
